source.title: Probing out-of-distribution generalization in machine learning for materials
source.authors: Kangming Li; Andre Niyongabo Rubungo; Xiangyun Lei; D. Persaud; Kamal Choudhary; Brian L. DeCost; Adji Bousso Dieng; J. Hattrick-Simpers

record.file_problem: The full paper and supplemental material are present. The code-availability statement contains a placeholder rather than a repository URL.
record.tranche_reason: The study varies training time and training-set size for materials-property models and reports that scaling can fail or worsen OOD performance, refining and challenging the broader scaling-law idea in this new setting. It does not test language-model cross-entropy scaling or compute-optimal parameter/token allocation.
record.gate_note: The paper evaluates materials formation-energy MAE, not language-model held-out cross-entropy. It does not sweep parameter count or compute, fit power laws, test small-run extrapolation, or optimize a parameter/token split. Its general OOD scores, representation analyses, and comparisons among model architectures are not scaling-learning-curve results and are omitted.
record.test_reason: In a new setting (materials formation-energy regression with graph neural network and tree models), the study varies training-set size from about 10^2 to 10^6 and reports in-distribution and out-of-distribution MAE learning curves. This bears on whether scaling behaviour carries over beyond text pretraining (V5). It fits no power law, and its 'training time' curves come from fixed-data, fixed-model runs, so they are not compute scaling.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. Scaling data or training time helps when test data are representationally in-domain, but is marginal or adverse for representationally OOD tasks. Heuristic OOD tests therefore overstate generalizability and the benefits of scaling.
record.recipe_differences: The original studies examine language-model loss and scaling in parameters, tokens, or compute. This paper trains materials-property models and measures formation-energy MAE while varying training time or training-set size, with OOD tasks defined by material chemistry or structure. It does not fit power laws or optimize compute allocation.
record.method_sensitivity: Outcome varies with representational domain and OOD task; training time versus training-set size; dataset (Materials Project, JARVIS, OQMD); and model/task combination.

fits_no_version.finding: With data and model fixed, OOD MAE falls for about 20 boosting rounds or epochs, then rises or plateaus, while ID MAE keeps falling (XGB leave-F, GMP leave-O, ALIGNN leave-H on JARVIS).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Longer training on fixed data can degrade out-of-distribution error even as in-distribution error improves.

record.problems: The study uses materials-property MAE rather than language-model cross-entropy and does not fit power laws; most learning-curve values are shown in figures without uncertainty estimates. Hyperparameters were tuned on an in-distribution validation set and reused across OOD tasks rather than tuned separately for each task.
record.rows_left_out: Other learning curves across models and tasks appear in Supplemental Figs. 15–21. They were not separately extracted because the main text reports the representative tasks and broader trend; the supplemental curves do not add stated numeric results beyond those represented here.

untested.parts: Fitted power-law form and exponents; scaling in model size or compute; image/video modalities; repeated-data, fine-tuning and transfer regimes.
All: no shape sweep at fixed parameter count.
All: no comparison of fitted exponents.

missing.what: ID test MAE versus training-set size for ALIGNN (dashed baseline curves), as their own rows; the paper says it decreases continuously
XGB MAE versus training-set size on MP and OQMD, including leave-one-space-group-out tasks
OOD MAE for the ≥5-element task is below the ID test MAE

record.verdict_notes: This is a materials-science study measuring formation-energy MAE, not language-model loss. The authors frame their OOD results as 'violations of neural scaling laws', but the scaling-law versions concern held-out loss from the training distribution, so the OOD findings narrow V5 rather than refute it. Training-time rows were unlinked because they come from fixed-data, fixed-model runs. Code is not released (placeholder link).

versions.untested_parts: Language-model held-out pretraining cross-entropy versus parameters, tokens, or compute; power-law behavior across several orders of magnitude.
Extrapolation from power laws fitted on small language-model runs to much larger runs.
Fixed-compute optimization of parameter and token counts and their scaling with compute.
Architecture variation at fixed parameter count and its effect on language-model loss.

The study tests scaling behavior for materials-property prediction using MAE versus training time or training-set size, but does not fit or establish power-law forms. It does not test image/video modalities, repeated data, fine-tuning, or transfer in language models.
Downstream language-model task performance as a function of scale or pretraining loss.
The study does not compare fitted exponents or compute-optimal allocations across counting, scheduling, data, or fitting choices.

rows.subject: XGB
rows.operation_detail: Varied training time (boosting rounds) in the JARVIS leave-F-out task and measured formation-energy MAE.
rows.baseline: ID test MAE decreases with training time; exact values not stated
rows.value: OOD MAE decreases only during the initial 20 training rounds, then continuously increases with more training
rows.note: The result is explicitly described in the text; the plot provides the learning curve.
rows.check: XGB boosting rounds on a fixed dataset with a fixed model is overfitting over training time, not compute scaling with data and model non-bottlenecked. It does not measure what V1 or V5 names.

rows.subject: GMP
rows.operation_detail: Varied training time (epochs) in the JARVIS leave-O-out task and measured formation-energy MAE.
rows.baseline: ID MAE decreases with increasing training time; exact values not stated
rows.value: For representationally OOD tasks, OOD MAE tends to increase or remain constant beyond around 20 epochs
rows.note: The paper describes a similar pattern for the leave-O-out and leave-H-out tasks; the plotted curve is for GMP leave-O-out.
rows.check: GMP epochs on fixed data (200-epoch schedule) is a training-duration and overfitting curve, not a scaling-law axis. The value is the paper's generic statement about rep-OOD tasks, not a task-specific number.

rows.subject: ALIGNN
rows.operation_detail: Varied training time (epochs) in the JARVIS leave-H-out task and measured formation-energy MAE.
rows.baseline: ID MAE decreases with increasing training time; exact values not stated
rows.value: For representationally OOD tasks, OOD MAE tends to increase or remain constant beyond around 20 epochs
rows.note: The text says a similar pattern occurs for leave-H-out; the curve is shown for ALIGNN.
rows.check: Same issue as r2: ALIGNN epochs on fixed data is not compute scaling, and the value is a generic statement.

rows.subject: ALIGNN
rows.operation_detail: Varied training-set size and measured formation-energy MAE in the Materials Project leave-F-out task.
rows.measure: OOD formation-energy MAE versus training-set size
rows.baseline: ID performance consistently improves with increasing training-set size; exact values not stated
rows.value: Increasing training-set size from 10² to 10⁵ only further degrades the already bad OOD performance
rows.note: The direction and training-set-size range are stated in the text.
rows.check: Measure is OOD (distribution-shifted) MAE, not held-out same-distribution loss. ALIGNN was trained for a fixed 25 epochs with ID-tuned hyperparameters at all data sizes.

rows.subject: ALIGNN
rows.operation_detail: Varied training-set size and measured formation-energy MAE in the Materials Project leave-H-out task.
rows.measure: OOD formation-energy MAE versus training-set size
rows.baseline: ID performance consistently improves with increasing training-set size; exact values not stated
rows.value: A “V” shaped learning curve: MAE first decreases and then increases as training-set size grows
rows.note: The text explicitly describes the non-monotonic curve.
rows.check: V-shaped curve: error rises at the larger training sizes, so scaling reverses over the upper range. 'partial' understates this. No numbers are stated.

rows.subject: ALIGNN
rows.operation_detail: Varied training-set size and measured formation-energy MAE for structures with five or more elements in Materials Project.

conditions.value: test structures with ≥5 elements; training structures with fewer than 5 elements

rows.measure: OOD formation-energy MAE versus training-set size
rows.baseline: ID MAE decreases with increasing training-set size; exact values not stated
rows.value: MAE consistently decreases with increasing training-set size
rows.note: The authors interpret this task as mainly representationally in-domain, rather than evidence of difficult extrapolation.
rows.check: Direction only: MAE decreases monotonically. No power-law fit, so the power-law form itself is not confirmed.

rows.subject: ALIGNN
rows.operation_detail: Varied training-set size and measured formation-energy MAE in OQMD OOD tasks.

conditions.value: representationally OOD tasks; task-specific results in figure

rows.measure: OOD formation-energy MAE versus training-set size
rows.baseline: ID test MAE continues to decrease with training-set size; exact values not stated
rows.value: Increasing training-set size leads to only marginal improvement or degradation for test data outside the training domain
rows.note: The text reports the same trend on OQMD, described as about an order of magnitude larger than Materials Project.
rows.check: Generic statement covering several OQMD rep-OOD tasks (marginal gain or degradation). Task-level curves are only in Fig. 5(e) and Supp. Fig. 19.

rows.subject: ALIGNN
rows.operation_detail: Compared prediction-error distributions across training-set sizes in the OQMD leave-H-out task.
rows.baseline: OOD MAE at training-set size 10⁴; exact value not stated
rows.value: OOD MAE increases 5-fold when training-set size increases from 10⁴ to 10⁶; errors shift toward positive values and spread more widely
rows.note: The text attributes the shift to systematic overestimation enhanced by training on more data from the training domain.
rows.check: OK. The baseline should read OQMD leave-H-out OOD MAE at 10^4 training structures; a 5-fold increase is reached at 10^6.

relationships.condition: ALIGNN data scaling, test sets lying outside the representational training domain (MP leave-F/H-out; OQMD leave-H-out and other rep-OOD tasks)
relationships.reason: OOD MAE worsens, is V-shaped, or improves only marginally as training data grows, while ID MAE keeps falling (r4, r5, r7, r8). Data scaling does not carry over to distribution-shifted test data.
relationships.display_finding: Out-of-distribution MAE worsened, became V-shaped, or improved marginally as data increased, while in-distribution MAE continued falling.

relationships.condition: ALIGNN data scaling, test data mainly inside the representational domain (MP and OQMD ≥5-element structures; ID test sets)
relationships.reason: MAE decreases consistently with training-set size (r6, and the ID dashed curves in Fig. 5d-e). This supports direction only; the power-law form is not fitted.
relationships.display_finding: MAE decreased consistently with training-set size for tests mainly inside the representational domain, without a fitted power law.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: challenges
reader_labels.condition: Representationally OOD materials-property tasks, including the reported leave-F-out and leave-H-out cases
reader_labels.reason: Increasing training time or training-set size can worsen OOD MAE or produce a non-monotonic curve rather than consistent improvement (r1, r4, r5, r8); the authors state that scaling benefits for these tasks are marginal or adverse (r2, r3, r7). This tests scaling trends, not a fitted power-law form.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Tasks whose test data are mainly representationally in-domain, including the ≥5-elements Materials Project task
reader_labels.reason: The reported MAE decreases with training-set size in this task, while the paper says scaling laws are valid for representationally ID generalization; this does not establish a power-law form (r6).
